doc.title: Longineu Parsons interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 17, 2026

title: Coltrane, rules as performance practices, and seeking new ways
summary: The raw emotion and freedom of Coltrane appealed to him; he argues rules are only performance practices and cites Threadgill, Oliver Lake, Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra as seekers of new ways.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: So what did you think – I had an experience with Coltrane. I was into Paul Desmond and then Cannonball but someone said, “Oh you’ve got to listen to John Coltrane.” And unwittingly I went to a record store and I bought the LP called “Om” and it scared me at first. And I did not listen to him for a while until “My Favorite Things.” But what was it about “Expressions” that hit you in the heart?

The raw emotion and the freedom of it. He was free to express what he was feeling. He didn’t allow any of the so-called “rules” to get in the way. See when we are studying music, like as an academic I can tell you there’s rules this and rules that. And that’s B.S. There’s no such thing as a rule. These are performance practices. And then people came along and said this is the rule because if you’re doing Baroque music and Baroque counterpoint this is how J.S. Bach did it. Basically what they’re saying, “Therefore this is the rule.” Okay so we learn okay American song form. Okay the rules are like this. This chord means – suggests this scale or these potential scales, these chords. Okay so we learn these things and this is how it’s supposed to go. But these are somebody else’s inventions, somebody else saying this is how they do it. It’s good to know this, it’s good to be able to use this, but at the same time why do I need to be restricted to it? Because what if I want to employ say some of the twelve-tone work of Arnold Schoenberg that has spent plenty of time studying and learning how to do. You know as part of my final, my doctorate is in classical composition. My masters is in classical trumpet. But the masters is actually both and then the doctorate is composition but with trumpet as the side thing. So if I’m playing a tune like a regular jazz tune, which, you know most of the time © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

American song form from some show or whatever, okay, great song, great pieces of work. As a classical composer it’s not all that exciting to me. So I’m looking at how I can bring all of this together. And thinking about people like Henry Threadgill and thinking about people like Oliver Lake and the people I played with, well especially Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra. They’re looking for ways to do things, for new ways. Or finding ways to just express who they are. And why should that expression be restricted to what others have done before?
